Definition
In this lesson, we will look at the operation and usage of math instructions. Math instructions allow you to manipulate data in the PLC memory.
SUB - SUBTRACT
MUL - MULTIPLY
DIV - DIVIDE
DDV - DOUBLE DIVIDE
NEG - NEGATE
CLR - CLEAR
TOD - CONVERT TO BCD
Math instructions include adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing, just to name a few. By manipulating data with these instructions, you can calculate many different things.
In the experiment, you will enter a ladder logic program that demonstrates the operation of math instructions.
Let's begin the lesson on MATH INSTRUCTIONS...............................
LESSON MENU
MATH INSTRUCTIONSLE
While obtaining data in a ladder logic program is important, the values you obtain may not directly tell you the information you would like to know.
DISCUSSION
Some information may be acquired only by mathematical operation using the values obtained by the ladder logic program.

Let's say you have a different sensor that returns the paint rate of flow from the nozzle. Now you can divide the number of triangles by the rate of paint flow to get a value that does not depend on paint rate........
You can see how the other variables in the system affect the rate at which the triangles get painted.
There are hundreds of different uses for the math instructions. The way they are used depends on the process you are writing ladder logic for and the data that you obtain.
The list below shows all the math instructions that we will examine in this lesson. Notice that there are quite a few math instructions.
SUB - SUBTRACT
MUL - MULTIPLY
DIV - DIVIDE
DDV - DOUBLE DIVIDE
NEG - NEGATE
CLR - CLEAR
TOD - CONVERT TO BCD
The first instruction is the Add (ADD) instruction. This instruction requires three parameters: source A, source B, and a destination. Source A is added to source B and stored at the destination.....
Carry ( C ) - High if carry, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise

The sources contain the two values that will be added. One of these can be a permanent value that you have entered, known as a constant, but at least one of them must point to a data word in memory...
The destination is the location where you would like the result of the addition to be stored. This, too, must be a data word in memory.
Something that you may not have seen before are the arithmetic status bits. These are stored in the S data file. These bits are affected by many math instructions.

The bits are used to inform you about the result of the operation that you performed, in this case, the addition instruction. The arithmetic status bits are Carry (C), Overflow (V), Zero (Z), and Sign (S).

A word is only 16 bits long. When the Add instruction is used, the result of adding two 16-bit numbers is often a 17 bit value. Since only 16 bits can be stored in the destination register, the PLC sets the carry bit high. If the result is only 16 bits, the PLC sets the carry bit to zero...
Carry ( C ) - High if carry, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise
The next status bit is the overflow bit. The overflow bit is set when you add two positive or negative values which result in an incorrect value because it moved out of the allowable range.
Carry ( C ) - High if carry, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise

The example below shows the overflow condition. Two positive values are added, and a negative value results. The range of an integer is -32,768 to 32,767. If added or subtracted numbers are outside that range, the overflow bit is set...
Also, the PLC will place either -32,768 or 32,767 in the destination location, depending on which end of the range you overflowed.
The next status bit is the zero bit. If the result of the addition is zero, this bit is set high. If the result of the addition is not zero, this bit is set low.
Carry ( C ) - High if carry, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise
The last arithmetic status bit is the sign bit. This bit is set high if the result is a negative value, and it is set low if the result is a positive value.
Carry ( C ) - High if carry, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise
The next instruction is the Subtract (SUB) instruction. This instruction requires the same parameters as the Add instruction. Source B is subtracted from source A and stored in the destination...
Carry ( C ) - High if borrow, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if underflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise

The arithmetic status bits are set differently for the Subtract instruction. The carry bit is set high if the subtraction required a borrow from the 17 bit. If no borrow was required, this bit is set low......
Carry ( C ) - High if borrow, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if underflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise
The overflow bit actually indicates an underflow. This is the condition where subtracting two numbers goes out of the
-32,768 to 32,767 range. If the subtraction result is outside this range, the overflow bit, representing an underflow, will be set...
Carry ( C ) - High if borrow, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if underflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise
Also, depending on the side of the range you underflow, either
-32,768 or 32,767 will be placed in the destination location.
Both the zero and sign bits of the arithmetic status bits are set the same as they are with the Add instruction......
Carry ( C ) - High if borrow, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if underflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise

This instruction is the Multiply (MUL) instruction, which requires the same parameters as the Add and Subtract instructions. Source A is multiplied by source B with the product placed in the destination and the Math Register...
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee

The math register consists of two 16-bit words in the S data file. These two words make one 32-bit value. If an overflow occurs in the multiplication for the 16-bit destination, the correct 32-bit result will be in the math register...

The zero and sign bits work the same as in the previously described instructions. The carry bit is not used and is always cleared. The overflow bit operates the same as the previously described instructions; however, the correct result can still be obtained from the math register..
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee

This is the Divide (DIV) instruction. Source A is divided by source B with the result placed in the destination and the math register. In the destination, the result of the division is stored and rounded up if the remainder is greater than 0.5...
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow or divide by zero, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise, undefined on overflow
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflow
In the math register, the unrounded result is stored in the high word and the remainder is stored in the low word.
The carry bit is always set to zero. The overflow bit is set high if the result is outside the -32,768 to 32,767 range or if divide by zero occurs. Remember, math does not allow division by zero.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow or divide by zero, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise, undefined on overflow
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflow
The zero bit is set high if the result is zero, low if not zero, and undefined if an overflow occurs. Undefined means the value of this bit is unknown.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow or divide by zero, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise, undefined on overflow
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflow
The sign bit is set high if the result is negative, low if the result is positive, and, again, undefined if an overflow occurs.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow or divide by zero, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise, undefined on overflow
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflow

The next instruction is the Double Divide (DDV) instruction. This instruction allows you to divide bigger numbers by using the math register. When this instruction is executed, the entire math register is divided by the source in the instruction...
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow or divide by zero, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
The result is placed in the destination and math register, just as it was with the other divide instruction.

The carry bit is always set to zero. Overflow is set high on divide by zero or a result that is outside the -32,768 to 32,767 range. The zero bit is high for a zero result and low otherwise. The sign bit is high for a negative result, low for positive result, and undefined if overflow is set...
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow or divide by zero, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
This is the Negate (NEG) instruction. This instruction is used to change the sign of the source and place it in the destination. The example below demonstrates this operation.
Carry ( C ) - Set low if results is zero or overflow, high otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww

The carry bit is set low if the result is zero or an overflow occurs; otherwise, it is set high. The overflow bit is set high if an overflow occurs as described earlier, and the value 32,767 is placed in the destination...
Carry ( C ) - Set low if results is zero or overflow, high otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
The zero bit is high for a zero result and low when not zero. The sign bit is high for a negative result and low for a positive result.
Carry ( C ) - Set low if results is zero or overflow, high otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
Which instruction is used to divide the value in the math register by a source value and place the result in the math register and destination?
Remember, it is the Double Divide instruction that is used to divide larger values stored in the 32-bit math register.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow or divide by zero, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
TRY AGAIN!
The next instruction is the Clear (CLR) instruction. This is used to set a destination to zero. The only parameter for this instruction is the destination data location.
When this instruction is evaluated, the carry bit, overflow bit, and sign bit are set low. The zero bit is set high.
The next two instructions convert decimal values stored in data files to or from binary coded decimal (BCD). As you may remember, BCD is just another way to encode data.
SUB - SUBTRACT
MUL - MULTIPLY
DIV - DIVIDE
DDV - DOUBLE DIVIDE
NEG - NEGATE
CLR - CLEAR
TOD - CONVERT TO BCD

The PLC may obtain BCD data from an external device. This must be converted to decimal in order to perform other math operations on it. If you need to send the data back to the device, you may need the data to be in BCD format............
This instruction is the Convert to BCD (TOD) instruction. This instruction requires a source and a destination. The example below illustrates a BCD conversion.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if result is larger than 9999
Zero ( Z ) - Set if destination value is zero
Sign ( S ) - Set if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww

The carry bit is always set low. The overflow bit is set high if the converted BCD value is greater than 9999; otherwise, it is set low. The zero bit is set high if the result is zero and set low otherwise...
Overflow ( V ) - Set if result is larger than 9999
Zero ( Z ) - Set if destination value is zero
Sign ( S ) - Set if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
The sign bit is set high if the source is negative and low if the source is positive. Notice that it is the source that is being checked, not the result.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if result is larger than 9999
Zero ( Z ) - Set if destination value is zero
Sign ( S ) - Set if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
If you use the math register as the destination, you can convert into a 5-digit BCD value. The overflow bit will still be set high.
This instruction is the Convert from BCD (FRD) instruction. This instruction will convert a BCD value to a decimal value. A source and a destination are required..............
Overflow ( V ) - Set if result is not BCD or overflow
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero,low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Low if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
If the math register is used as the source, a five-digit BCD value can be converted; otherwise, only a four-digital BCD value can be converted.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if result is not BCD or overflow
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero,low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Low if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
The carry bit is always set low. The overflow bit is set high if the value being converted is not a BCD value or the resulting BCD value is greater than 32,767. Otherwise, it is set to low.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if result is not BCD or overflow
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero,low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Low if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
The zero bit is set high for a zero result and low when not zero. The sign bit is always set low.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if result is not BCD or overflow
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero,low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Low if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww

The next instruction is the Decode 4 to 1 of 16 (DCD). This instruction requires a source and destination. The code is used to set only one bit high at a time in the destination based on the lower half of the lower byte value in the source....

In other words, the lowest 4 bits in the source, 0, 1, 2, and 3 can represent a value between 0 and 15. The value you have set in the source will turn on that particular bit in the destination and set all the reset to low...
Illustrated below are two examples of this instruction. Notice how only the lower 4 bits of the source determine which bit is high in the destination...............

This table shows all combinations used in the source and the result in the destination. This instruction could be used to turn on 1 output of 16, one at a time. This instruction does not use the math register, and the arithmetic status bits remain unchanged...
DECODE TABLE
SOURCE DESTINATION
The next instruction is the Square Root (SQR) instruction. This instruction takes the square root of the value in the source and places it in the destination.
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero,low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Lowsource is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww

The SQR instruction does not know whether the source is positive or negative, so it will determine a square root for negative numbers without giving you an error. It is important to note, however, the result will not be correct...
Before using this instruction, always use the Compare instruction to make sure the value is not negative..
The carry bit is reserved and should not be used with this instruction. The overflow bit and sign bit are always set low. The zero bit is set high when the result is zero and low when not zero...
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero,low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Lowsource is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
The last instruction is the Scale Data (SCL) instructions. This instruction is used to take data and scale its value up and down.
This instruction also allows you to add an offset to the result before it is stored at a destination.

In the example below, the source value is multiplied by 20000 and divided by 10000. This is the rate setting, sometimes referred to as the slope. Then an offset is added. The result is stored in the destination...

The carry bit is not used and is reserved by the instruction. The overflow bit is set high if an overflow occurs throughout the instruction. The zero bit is set high if the result is zero and low if not zero. The sign bit is set high if the result is negative and low if positive...
If the source value 0000 0000 0000 0110 was passed to the DCD instruction, what would be the result in the destination?

Remember, the DCD instruction will set only the bit represented by the lower four bits of the source. The lower four bits of the source equal 6, which would set bit six. Don't forget that the leftmost bit is bit 0, so the seventh bit from the left is bit six...

We have examined the math instructions used by the PLC in ladder logic programs. There are many different instructions that provide a variety of operations.
SUB - SUBTRACT
MUL - MULTIPLY
DIV - DIVIDE
DDV - DOUBLE DIVIDE
NEG - NEGATE
CLR - CLEAR
TOD - CONVERT TO BCD
The last thing to be mentioned deals with the overflow bit, which, as you know, can be set by many of the instructions.
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero,low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Low if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww

The overflow bit informs the PLC of a minor error. If you detect an overflow, you must set the overflow bit to low before the end of the ladder logic cycle. Otherwise, the PLC will cause a CPU fault and stop execution of the program...
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero,low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Low if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
The overflow bit allows you to deal with a result error before the PLC faults because of the result. The table below shows the bit locations of all the bits and the math register.

1. The Add (ADD) instruction is used to add two numbers and store the result in a destination location.
Carry ( C ) - High if carry, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise
2. The Subtract (SUB) instruction is used to subtract two numbers and store the result in a destination location.
Carry ( C ) - High if borrow, low otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if underflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise
3. The Multiply (MUL) instruction is used to multiply two values and store the result in a destination and the math register.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee
4. The Divide (DIV) instruction is used to divide one value by another and store the rounded result in a destination. The unrounded result and remainder are stored in the math register.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow or divide by zero, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise, undefined on overflow
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflow

5. The Double Divide (DDV) instruction is used to divide large values stored in the math register by another value specified as a source. The rounded result is placed in the destination and the unrounded result and remainder are stored in the math register.
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow or divide by zero, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
6. The Negate (NEG) instruction turns a number from positive to negative or from negative to positive.
Carry ( C ) - Set low if results is zero or overflow, high otherwise
Overflow ( V ) - Set if overflow, low otherwise
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero, low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Set if result is negative, low otherwise, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
7. The Clear (CLR) instruction places the number zero into a destination location.

Overflow ( V ) - Set if result is larger than 9999
Zero ( Z ) - Set if destination value is zero
Sign ( S ) - Set if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
Overflow ( V ) - Set if result is not BCD or overflow
Zero ( Z ) - Set if result is zero,low otherwise
Sign ( S ) - Low if source is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww
9. The Decode 4 to 1 of 16 (DCD) instruction is used to decode a 4-bit binary value to an individual bit of a 16-bit word.
10. The Square Root (SQR) instruction takes the square root of a source value and places it in a destination.

Sign ( S ) - Lowsource is negative, low otherwiseeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee, undefined on overflowwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww

Definition
The program below is the ladder logic you will enter to demonstrate the math instructions.

Before we actually begin entering the program into the PLC APS software, let's look at what the program should do. This will help you understand if the program is operating properly when we are testing it...

On the 5050-1 PC card, there are three switches that we will use for this program: two push button switches and a slide switch. In the program, there are two counters. The values stored in the counters will be summed using the ADD instruction...
The START and STOP buttons are used to increment or decrement the counter. The slide switch controls which counter the START and STOP buttons change.

The first rung in the ladder logic program checks to see if the START button is pushed and that the slide switch is in the ON position. If these conditions are met, counter 0 is incremented with the CTU instruction...

Notice the preset value is zero. We are not counting to a particular number, so the done bit has no meaning for us. For convenience, we have set the preset to zero to remind us we do not need the done bit...

The next rung determines whether the STOP button is pushed in and the slide switch is in the ON position. If a true logic path can be traced through these two bit instructions, counter 0 will be decremented by 1...
Rung 3 determines whether the START button is pressed in and the slide switch is in the OFF position. If there is a true logic path through these bit instructions, counter 1 will be incremented by 1.
witch ON means START increments and STOP d , decrementing counter 0. Slide switch OFF means START and STOP increment, decrementing counter 1.

In Rung 4, the STOP button and the slide switch are off, causing counter 1 to decrement by 1. Remember, slide switch ON means START increments and STOP decrements counter 0. Slide switch OFF means START increments and STOP decrements counter 1.1..ing counter 1.

In the next rung, we have the ADD instruction. This instruction adds the accumulator of counter 0 to the accumulator of counter 1. Recall that the accumulator is the second word of a counter data file..file...
The destination setting of the ADD instruction sends the result to output port 0, the LEDs of the PLC Trainer.
As the ladder logic program is evaluated, the LEDs of the PLC Trainer will indicate the addition of counter 0's accumulator value and counter 1's accumulator value.
The value represented on the LEDs will be in binary. The maximum number that can be displayed on the LEDs is 255.
If the result of adding the counter values exceeds 255, the LED output will be incorrect. Remember, the actual accumulators can be counted from -32,768 to 32,767.

The program below is the ladder logic program you will enter to demonstrate the math instructions.

Before we actually begin entering the program into the PLC RSLogix software, let's look at what the program should do. This will help you understand if the program is operating properly when we are testing it...

On the 5050-1 PC card, there are three switches that we will use for this program: two push button switches and a slide switch. In our program, there are two counters. The values stored in the counters will be summed using the ADD instruction.
TUPTTQTT
The START and STOP push buttons are used to increment or decrement the counter. The slide switch controls which counter the START and STOP buttons change.

The first rung of the ladder logic program checks to see if the START button is pushed and that the slide switch is in the ON position. If these conditions are met, counter 0 is incremented with the CTU instruction..

Notice the preset value is zero. We are not counting to a particular number, so the done bit has no meaning for us. For convenience, we have set the preset to zero to remind us we do not need the done bit...

The next rung determines whether the STOP button is pressed and the slide switch is in the ON position. If a true logic path can be traced through these two bit instructions, counter 0 will be decremented by 1..
Rung 3 determines whether the START button is pressed and the slide switch is in the OFF position. If there is a true logic path through these bit instructions, counter 1 will be incremented by 1.
In Rung 4, the STOP button is pressed and the slide switch is in the OFF position, which causes the counter to decrement by 1.
Remember, slide switch ON means START increments and STOP decrements counter 0. Slide switch OFF means START increments and STOP decrements counter 1.
TUPTTQTT

In the last rung, we have the ADD instruction. This instruction adds the accumulator of counter 0 to the accumulator of counter 1. Recall that the accumulator is the second word of a counter data file.
The destination setting of the ADD instruction sends the result to output port 0, the LEDs of the PLC trainer.
As the ladder logic program is evaluated, the LEDs of the PLC Trainer will indicate the addition of counter 0's accumulator value and counter 1's accumulator value.
The value represented on the LEDs will be in binary. The maximum number that can be displayed on the LEDs is 255.
If the result of adding the counter values exceeds 255, the LED output will be incorrect. Remember, the actual accumulators can be counted from -32,768 to 32,767.
